At one point in the impact statement it is stated, "For instance, in a balanced ecosystem a predator may be responsible for limiting the population of a herbivore, which in turn limits the growth of certain plants." This statement, I believe, is misleading, and in a general context it may be incorrect.
Some of the most respected work on predator-prey relationships, primarily that of Dr. Paul Errington, points out the security of the prey species' habitat governs the number of animals that will eventually survive. Predation, much like harvest by hunters, only removes the annual surplus, or those individuals that are forced to live on marginal habitat due to population density increases.
The controlling factors are in the security of the prey species' habitat, and not in the predator's ability to occasionally or even regularly commit a depredation upon an individual of a prey species population.
In closing, I would suggest that we recommend to the authors of this impact statement and the federal legislation in question that they concentrate their efforts on habitat management and leave the regulating of resident wildlife populations to the state, as they suggest in the proposed Animal Damage Control Act of 1972, also in this office for review.
JAMES A. POSEWITZ, CHIEF
ENVIRONMENTAL RESOURCES DIVISION
